authority: Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment (DETE)
field_label: General Employment Permit (GEP) or Critical Skills Employment Permit (CSEP)
non_obvious_official_guidance: DETE states both GEP and CSEP are available to non-EEA nationals and are applied for online via EPOS.
non_obvious_actual_reality: CSEP is tied to the individual (not the employer) and requires the occupation to appear on the Critical Skills Occupations List at ≥€38,000 (listed roles) or ≥€64,000 (unlisted roles). GEP requires a Labour Market Needs Test (LMNT): the role must be advertised for at least 2 weeks nationally and 2 weeks on EURES before applying. Ireland is NOT in Schengen — a separate Irish work authorisation is always required even for EU-passport holders from non-EEA states. Employer must hold a valid Revenue tax registration and have no outstanding DETE compliance issues or the application is rejected outright.
non_obvious_action_required: Confirm occupations list eligibility before choosing permit type. If GEP required, document LMNT advertising dates and retain evidence. Verify employer's Revenue compliance status before submitting.

authority: Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) / Irish Naturalisation and Immigration Service (INIS)
non_obvious_official_guidance: ISD states visa-required nationals must hold a valid Irish visa prior to arrival.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Ireland is NOT in the Schengen Area. A Schengen visa does not permit entry to Ireland. Nationals of visa-required countries (e.g. India, China, Philippines, Brazil) who transit through a Schengen country en route to Ireland need both a Schengen transit visa AND a separate Irish 'D' entry visa. Processing times at Irish missions range from 4–12 weeks; priority processing is not consistently available. Visa-required employees who arrive without a valid Irish visa are refused entry regardless of permit status.
non_obvious_action_required: Check the ISD visa-required nationals list against the employee's passport nationality. Apply for the Irish 'D' long-stay visa well ahead of travel — do not assume a UK or Schengen visa covers Ireland. Include the employment permit approval letter in the visa application.

authority: Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) / Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB)
form_name: IRP Registration — online appointment via ISD portal
field_label: Irish Residence Permit (IRP) — Stamp 1 (employment permit holder)
non_obvious_official_guidance: ISD requires non-EEA nationals to register their immigration permission within 90 days of arrival.
non_obvious_actual_reality: IRP registration in Dublin is handled by the Burgh Quay Registration Office — appointment slots are heavily oversubscribed and typically book out 3–6 weeks in advance. The employee must book online immediately upon arrival, not at day 85. The registration fee is €300 payable by card in person. The resulting IRP card (biometric credit-card format) is required to open an Irish bank account, sign a lease, and access most services — it is not optional admin.
non_obvious_action_required: Book the IRP registration appointment online on or before arrival day — do not wait. Bring: valid passport, employment permit, proof of Irish address, employer letter on headed paper, and €300. Outside Dublin, contact the local Garda district headquarters to register.

form_name: PPSN application — in person at Intreo Centre by appointment
Revenue myAccount — online registration at revenue.ie
field_label: myAccount registration to activate Revenue Payroll Notification (RPN)
non_obvious_official_guidance: Revenue states employees should register for myAccount so the employer can receive a Revenue Payroll Notification (RPN) and apply the correct tax credits and rate bands.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Without a registered myAccount and a live RPN, payroll software defaults to emergency tax regardless of the employee's actual income level. Personal tax credits (€1,875 personal credit + €1,875 employee credit = €3,750 total in 2024), the standard-rate cut-off point (€42,000 at 20%), and any reliefs are not applied until the RPN is active. The PPSN is required to register for myAccount, creating a sequencing dependency: IRP → PPSN → myAccount → RPN → correct tax.
non_obvious_action_required: Register for myAccount immediately after obtaining the PPSN. Provide the PPSN to the employer's payroll before the first pay date so the system can pull the RPN. If the first payrun has already run under emergency tax, the employer can pull a corrective RPN and apply the refund in the next pay cycle without requiring a separate Revenue claim.

form_name: N/A — payroll system default applied by employer
field_label: Emergency Tax — PAYE applied in absence of a valid RPN
deadline_label: Resolve within 4 weeks of first employment; financial impact from week 1
non_obvious_official_guidance: Revenue states employers must apply emergency tax rates when no RPN has been received for a new employee.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Emergency tax rates are severe and escalate: weeks 1–4 apply 20% PAYE with zero tax credits; from week 5, 40% PAYE on ALL income with no credits and no standard-rate band. USC is simultaneously applied at the highest 8% rate from week 1 under emergency rules. A mid-range employee earning €60,000/year can lose €800–€1,500+ more than normal in a single monthly payrun under emergency conditions. Many new arrivals are unaware this is happening until they receive their first payslip.
non_obvious_action_required: Obtain PPSN and register for myAccount before the first payrun without exception. If emergency tax has been deducted, do not file a separate Revenue refund claim — the employer's payroll system will auto-correct once the RPN is active and refund the over-deduction in the next pay cycle. If the employer cannot pull the RPN, the employee can use myAccount interactive return (Form 12) to reclaim excess.
source: Revenue — Emergency Tax and Universal Social Charge

form_name: N/A — applied through payroll; rates set by Revenue
non_obvious_official_guidance: Revenue states USC applies to gross income over €13,000/year at rates of 0.5%, 2%, 4%, and 8% depending on band (2024 rates).
non_obvious_actual_reality: USC is a wholly separate charge on top of PAYE income tax and PRSI — it cannot be offset by pension contributions or most tax credits (unlike PAYE). Medical card holders pay a capped 2% USC. Under emergency tax, USC defaults to 8% on all income from week 1 regardless of band, compounding the financial impact significantly. Internationally mobile employees present in Ireland for only part of the year are still liable on Irish-source income for the full USC bands — split-year treatment does not automatically reduce USC liability.
non_obvious_action_required: Ensure the RPN is active before the first payrun so correct USC bands are applied. If the employee holds a medical card, notify the employer to cap USC at 2%. Employees with split tax-year situations (arriving mid-year) should seek professional advice on USC liability for the Irish portion of the year.

form_name: GP registration — direct with individual GP practice
field_label: GP Registration / GMS Card eligibility check
non_obvious_official_guidance: HSE states all persons resident in Ireland are entitled to access public health services; GMS medical card provides free GP visits for those below income thresholds.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Ireland does not have universal free-at-point-of-use primary care for working adults above GMS income limits. Standard GP visits cost €50–€80 per consultation. Non-EEA employment permit holders on Stamp 1 have full access to public hospital services (emergency and inpatient) but pay GP fees privately. A GP Visit Card (lower income threshold than full GMS) provides free GP visits. Dublin GP practices accepting new patients have waiting lists of 4–8 weeks — registering before illness is essential. EU/EEA employees should carry their EHIC for temporary cover while an Irish card is arranged.
non_obvious_action_required: Use the HSE GP finder to locate practices accepting new patients and register immediately on arrival — not when sick. EU/EEA employees: carry EHIC from home country and apply for Irish EHIC before departure. Check eligibility for GMS or GP Visit Card via Intreo/DSP based on household income.

form_name: RTB Tenancy Registration — submitted by landlord
field_label: Tenancy Registration / Rent Pressure Zone (RPZ) rights
deadline_label: Landlord must register within 1 month of tenancy start
non_obvious_official_guidance: RTB states landlords must register new tenancies within 1 month of commencement; tenants hold rights under the Residential Tenancies Acts 2004–2022.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The Irish rental market, particularly Dublin, is extremely supply-constrained. Most landlords require proof of employment (offer letter or payslips), 3–6 months' deposit plus first month's rent upfront, and an Irish bank account — creating a compounding problem for new arrivals who have not received their first payslip and cannot open a bank account without an IRP card. Many landlords decline tenants on employment permits without an Irish guarantor. Rent Pressure Zone caps limit annual increases to 2% but do not constrain initial asking rents. Short-term furnished Airbnb-style accommodation is typically necessary as a 4–8 week bridge.
non_obvious_action_required: Prepare a rental application pack before departure: employer offer letter on headed paper, employment contract, previous landlord reference (certified translation if required), and photo ID. Open a digital bank account (N26, Revolut) immediately on arrival using the IRP card as identity verification. Budget for 1–2 months of bridge accommodation. Request a formal employer letter confirming salary, start date, and contract type for prospective landlords.

form_name: Form 12 (PAYE taxpayer) or Form 11 (self-assessed) — annual income tax return
field_label: Irish Tax Residence Determination — 183-day and 280-day rules
deadline_label: Assessed annually; first tax year is critical for split-year treatment
non_obvious_official_guidance: Revenue states an individual is tax resident in Ireland if present for 183+ days in a tax year, or 280+ combined days in the current and preceding year (with at least 30 days in each).
non_obvious_actual_reality: Irish tax residence is legally separate from 'ordinary residence' (resident for 3 consecutive years) and 'domicile' — and the combination determines the taxable scope. A non-ordinarily-resident, non-domiciled individual is taxed on Irish-source income plus any foreign income remitted to Ireland (remittance basis), not on worldwide income. Arriving mid-year can create a split-year treatment opportunity (reducing the Irish portion of the residence year) but it is not automatic — it must be claimed in the annual return. Tax treaty tie-breaker provisions must be invoked where the employee is simultaneously resident in Ireland and a treaty country.
non_obvious_action_required: Track days of Irish presence from arrival date. In the first tax year, a tax adviser should assess split-year treatment, remittance basis eligibility, ordinary residence status, and the applicable double-tax treaty. File the annual return by 31 October (paper) or mid-November via ROS (online filers) of the year following the tax year. Value withheld — individual determination required.

form_name: N/A — Class A PRSI deducted through payroll; A1/E101 via home-country authority for posted workers
field_label: Pay Related Social Insurance (PRSI) — class, entitlements, and totalization
deadline_label: Applies from first payrun; A1 certificate required before or on arrival if applicable
non_obvious_official_guidance: DSP states PRSI is collected through payroll at Class A (4% employee / 11.15% employer for most employees) and funds access to Jobseeker's Benefit, Illness Benefit, State Pension Contributory, and other benefits.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Employees sent from an EU/EEA country on assignment may remain subject to their home country's social security under EU Regulation 883/2004 — in which case they must hold a valid Form A1 issued by their home country authority before starting work in Ireland. Without the A1, the employer must deduct Irish Class A PRSI, potentially resulting in double social security contributions in both countries. Non-EU/EEA employees should check whether a bilateral totalization agreement exists between Ireland and their home country (Ireland has agreements with the US, Canada, Australia, Japan, South Korea, and others). Employment permit holders on Stamp 1 pay full Class A PRSI and accumulate contributions, but the Habitual Residence Condition (HRC) may restrict access to certain means-tested benefits.
non_obvious_action_required: For EU/EEA employees on assignment: obtain Form A1 from the home country social security authority confirming continued home-country coverage — this exempts them from Irish PRSI. For non-EU/EEA nationals: check the bilateral agreement list. Retain all payslips as evidence of Irish PRSI contributions paid for future aggregation or benefit claims. Value withheld — individual determination required.

authority: Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment (DETE)
form_name: Employment Permit Renewal — EPOS online application
field_label: GEP / CSEP Renewal — submitted up to 16 weeks before expiry
deadline_label: Apply no later than 16 weeks before permit expiry
non_obvious_official_guidance: DETE states renewal applications can be submitted up to 16 weeks before the current permit expires; permits can be renewed for up to 3 years.
non_obvious_actual_reality: If the employment permit lapses by even one day, the employee has no legal entitlement to work in Ireland and must immediately stop working. The IRP card validity is linked to the permit — an expired permit simultaneously invalidates the Stamp and can trigger immigration non-compliance findings. DETE renewal processing times currently range from 4–12 weeks and are not guaranteed. There is no automatic stay of work authorisation during renewal processing unless the renewal was submitted in-time. GEP holders who change employer require a brand-new GEP before starting with the new employer — they cannot begin work in reliance on the existing permit. CSEP holders can change employer after their first year without a new permit but must notify DETE.
non_obvious_action_required: Set a firm calendar reminder at 16 weeks before permit expiry — not week 12. Both employer and employee must submit renewal supporting documents via EPOS together. After the permit is renewed, book an IRP renewal appointment at ISD (allow 4 additional weeks for the appointment). Do not allow either the permit or the IRP to expire. Value withheld for immigration determination — individual advice required.
